{{Use American English|date = February 2019}}
{{Short description|"Smoothing" integral transform}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Weierstrass transform'''<ref>Ahmed I. Zayed, ''Handbook of Function and Generalized Function Transformations'', Chapter 18. CRC Press, 1996.</ref> of a [[function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f : \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}</math>, named after [[Karl Weierstrass]], is a "smoothed" version of <math>f(x)</math> obtained by averaging the values of <math>f</math>, weighted with a Gaussian centered at <math>x</math>.

[[Image:Weierstrass transform.svg|thumb|right|400px|The graph of a function <math>f(x)</math> (black) and its generalized Weierstrass transforms for five <math>t</math> parameters. The standard Weierstrass transform <math>F(x)</math> is given by the case <math>t=1</math> (in green)]]

Specifically, it is the function <math>F</math> defined by,
:<math>\!F(x) = \int\limits_{-\infty}^\infty f(y) \; e^{-\frac{(x-y)^2}{4}} \; \frac{dy}{\sqrt{4\pi}} = \int\limits_{-\infty}^\infty f(x-y) \; e^{-\frac{y^2}{4}} \; \frac{dy}{\sqrt{4\pi}},</math>
which is the [[convolution]] of <math>f</math> with the [[Gaussian function]], <math display="inline">e^{-x^2/4}/\sqrt{4\pi}.</math>

The factor <math display="inline">(4\pi)^{-1/2}</math> is chosen so that the Gaussian will have a total integral of 1, with the consequence that constant functions are not changed by the Weierstrass transform.

Instead of <math>F(x)</math>  one also writes <math>W[f](x)</math>. Note that <math>F(x)</math> need not exist for every real number <math>x</math>, when the defining integral fails to converge.

The Weierstrass transform is intimately related to the [[heat equation]] (or, equivalently, the [[diffusion equation]] with constant diffusion coefficient). If the function <math>f</math> describes the initial temperature at each point of an infinitely long rod that has constant [[thermal conductivity]] equal to 1, then the temperature distribution of the rod <math>t=1</math> time units later will be given by the function <math>F</math>. By using values of <math>t</math> different from 1, we can define the '''generalized Weierstrass transform''' of <math>f</math>.

The generalized Weierstrass transform provides a means to approximate a given integrable function <math>f</math> arbitrarily well with [[analytic function]]s.

==Names==
Weierstrass used this transform in his original proof of the [[Weierstrass approximation theorem]]. It is also known as the '''Gauss transform''' or '''Gauss–Weierstrass transform''' after [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] and as the '''Hille transform''' after [[Einar Carl Hille]] who studied it extensively. The generalization <math>W_t</math> mentioned below is known in [[signal analysis]] as a [[Gaussian filter]] and in [[image processing]] (when implemented on <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>) as a [[Gaussian blur]].

==Transforms of some important functions==

=== Constant Functions ===
Every [[constant function]] is its own Weierstrass transform. 

=== Polynomials ===
The Weierstrass transform of any [[polynomial]] is a polynomial of the same degree, and in fact has the same leading coefficient (the [[asymptotic growth]] is unchanged). 
Indeed, if <math>H_n</math> denotes the [[Hermite polynomials|(physicist's) Hermite polynomial]] of degree <math>n</math>, then the Weierstrass transform of <math>H_n(x/2)</math> is simply <math>x^n</math>. This can be shown by exploiting the fact that the [[generating function]] for the Hermite polynomials is closely related to the Gaussian kernel used in the definition of the Weierstrass transform.

=== Exponentials, Sines, and Cosines  ===
The Weierstrass transform of the exponential function <math>x \mapsto \exp(ax)</math> (where <math>a</math> is an arbitrary constant) is <math>x \mapsto \exp(a^2)\exp(ax)</math>. The function  <math>\exp(ax)</math> is thus an [[eigenfunction]] of the Weierstrass transform, with eigenvalue <math>\exp(a^2)</math>.{{NoteTag|More generally, <math>x \mapsto \exp(ax)</math> is an eigenfunction for ''any'' convolution transforms.}}

Using Weierstrass transform of <math>x \mapsto \exp(ax)</math> with <math>a =bi</math> where <math>b</math> is an arbitrary real constant and <math>i</math> is the [[imaginary unit]], and applying [[Euler's identity]], one sees that the Weierstrass transform of the function <math>\cos(bx)</math> is <math>\exp(-b^2)\cos(bx)</math> and the Weierstrass transform of the function <math>\sin(bx)</math> is <math> \exp(-b^2) \sin(bx)</math>.

=== Gaussian Functions  ===
The Weierstrass transform of the function <math>x \mapsto \exp(ax^2)</math> is 
<math display="block">
F(x) = \begin{cases}
  \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-4a}} \exp\left(\dfrac{ax^2}{1-4a}\right) & \text{if } a < 1/4 \\[5pt]
  \text{undefined} & \text{if } a \geq 1/4.
\end{cases}
</math> 
Of particular note is when <math>a</math> is chosen to be negative. If <math>a < 0</math>, then <math>\exp(ax^2)</math> is a Gaussian function and its Weierstrass transform is also a Gaussian function, but a "wider" one.

==General properties==
The Weierstrass transform assigns to each function <math>f</math> a new function <math>F</math>; this assignment is [[linear operator|linear]]. It is also translation-invariant, meaning that the transform of the function <math>f(x+a)</math> is <math>F(x+a)</math>. Both of these facts are more generally true for any [[integral transform]] defined via convolution.

If the transform <math>F(x)</math> exists for the real numbers <math>x=a</math> and <math>x=b</math>, then it also exists for all real values in between and forms an [[analytic function]] there; moreover, <math>F(x)</math> will exist for all [[complex number|complex]] values of <math>x</math> with <math>a \le \Re(x)\le b</math> and forms a [[holomorphic function]] on that strip of the [[complex plane]]. This is the formal statement of the "smoothness" of <math>F</math> mentioned above.

If <math>f</math> is integrable over the whole real axis (i.e. <math>f \in L^1(\R)</math>), then so is its Weierstrass transform <math>F</math>, and if furthermore <math>f(x)\ge 0</math> for all <math>x</math>, then also <math>F(x)\ge 0</math> for all <math>x</math> and the integrals of <math>f</math> and <math>F</math> are equal. This expresses the physical fact that the total thermal energy or [[heat]] is conserved by the heat equation, or that the total amount of diffusing material is conserved by the diffusion equation.

Using the above, one can show that for <math>1 \le p \le +\infty</math> and <math>f \in L^p(\R)</math>, we have <math>F \in L^p(\R)</math> and <math>\left\|F\right\|_p \le \left\|f\right\|_p</math>. The Weierstrass transform consequently yields a [[bounded operator]] <math>W : L^p(\R)\to L^p(\R)</math>.

If <math>f</math> is sufficiently smooth, then the Weierstrass transform of the <math>k</math>-th [[derivative]] of <math>f</math> is equal to the <math>k</math>-th derivative of the Weierstrass transform of <math>f</math>.

There is a formula relating the Weierstrass transform ''W'' and the [[two-sided Laplace transform]] <math>L</math>. If we define

:<math>g(x)=e^{-\frac{x^2}{4}} f(x)</math>

then

:<math>W[f](x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} e^{-x^2/4} L[g]\left(-\frac{x}{2}\right).</math>

=== Low-pass filter ===
{{details|Gaussian blur#Low-pass filter}}
We have seen above that the Weierstrass transform of <math>\cos(bx)</math> is <math>e^{-b^2}\cos(bx)</math>, and analogously for <math>\sin(bx)</math>. In terms of [[signal analysis]], this suggests that if the signal <math>f</math> contains the frequency <math>b</math> (i.e. contains a summand which is a combination of <math>\sin(bx)</math> and <math>\cos(bx)</math>), then the transformed signal <math>F</math> will contain the same frequency, but with an [[amplitude]] multiplied by the factor <math>e^{-b^2}</math>. This has the consequence that higher frequencies are reduced more than lower ones, and the Weierstrass transform thus acts as a [[low-pass filter]]. This can also be shown with the [[continuous Fourier transform]], as follows. The Fourier transform analyzes a signal in terms of its frequencies, transforms convolutions into products, and transforms Gaussians into Gaussians. The Weierstrass transform is convolution with a Gaussian and is therefore ''multiplication'' of the Fourier transformed signal with a Gaussian, followed by application of the inverse Fourier transform. This multiplication with a Gaussian in frequency space blends out high frequencies, which is another way of describing the "smoothing" property of the Weierstrass transform.

==The inverse transform==
The following formula, closely related to the [[Laplace transform]] of a Gaussian function, and a real analogue to the [[Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation]], is relatively easy to establish:

:<math>e^{u^2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-uy} e^{-y^2/4}\;dy.</math>

Now replace ''u'' with the formal differentiation operator ''D''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''d''/''dx'' and utilize the Lagrange [[shift operator]]  
:<math>e^{-yD}f(x)=f(x-y)</math>, 
(a consequence of the [[Taylor series]] formula and the definition of the [[exponential function]]), to obtain
:<math>
\begin{align}
e^{D^2}f(x) & = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-yD}f(x) e^{-y^2/4}\;dy \\
& =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x-y) e^{-y^2/4}\;dy=W[f](x)
\end{align}
</math>
to thus obtain the following formal expression for the Weierstrass transform <math>W</math>,
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation = <math>W=e^{D^2} ~,</math> 
|cellpadding= 6
|border
|border colour = #0073CF
|bgcolor=#F9FFF7}}
where the operator on the right is to be understood as acting on the function ''f''(''x'')  as
:<math>e^{D^2} f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{D^{2k}f(x)}{k!}~.</math>

The above formal derivation glosses over details of convergence, and the formula <math>W = e^{D^2}</math> is thus not universally valid; there are several functions <math>f</math> which have a well-defined Weierstrass transform, but for which <math>e^{D^2}(f)</math> cannot be meaningfully defined.

Nevertheless, the rule is still quite useful and can, for example, be used to derive the Weierstrass transforms of polynomials, exponential and [[trigonometric functions]] mentioned above.

The formal inverse of the Weierstrass transform is thus given by
:<math>W^{-1}=e^{-D^2}  ~. </math>
Again, this formula is not universally valid but can serve as a guide. It can be shown to be correct for certain classes of functions if the right-hand side operator is properly defined.<ref>G. G. Bilodeau, "[http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.dmj/1077470134 The Weierstrass Transform and Hermite Polynomials]". ''Duke Mathematical Journal'' 29 (1962), p. 293-308</ref>

One may, alternatively,  attempt to invert the Weierstrass transform in a slightly different way: given the analytic function
:<math>F(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n  ~,</math>
apply <math>W^{-1}</math> to obtain
:<math>f(x)=W^{-1}[F(x)]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n W^{-1}[x^n]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n H_n(x/2)</math>
once more using a fundamental property of the (physicists') [[Hermite polynomials]] <math>H_n</math>.

Again, this formula for <math>f(x)</math> is at best formal, since one didn't check whether the final series converges. But if, for instance, <math>f \in L^2(\R)</math>, then knowledge of all the derivatives of <math>F</math> at <math>x=0</math> suffices to yield the coefficients <math>a_n</math>; and to thus reconstruct <math>f</math> as a series of [[Hermite polynomials]].

A third method of inverting the Weierstrass transform exploits its connection to the Laplace transform mentioned above, and the well-known inversion formula for the Laplace transform. The result is stated below for distributions.

==Generalizations==
{{see also|Heat equation # Fundamental solutions|Heat kernel}}

We can use convolution with the Gaussian kernel <math display="block">\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi t}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{4t}}, \quad t > 0,</math> instead of <math display="block">\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{4}},</math> thus defining an operator {{math|''W<sub>t</sub>''}}, the generalized Weierstrass transform.

For small values of <math>t</math>, <math>W_t[f]</math> is very close to <math>f</math>, but smooth. The larger <math>t</math>, the more this operator averages out and changes <math>f</math>. Physically, <math>W_t</math> corresponds to following the heat (or diffusion) equation for <math>t</math> time units, and this is additive, 
<math display="block">W_s \circ W_t = W_{s+t},</math> 
corresponding to "diffusing for <math>t</math> time units, then <math>s</math> time units, is equivalent to diffusing for <math>s+t</math> time units". One can extend this to <math>t=0</math> by setting <math>W_0</math> to be the identity operator (i.e. convolution with the [[Dirac delta function]]), and these then form a [[one-parameter semigroup]] of operators.

The kernel <math display="block">\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi t}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{4t}},</math> used for the generalized Weierstrass transform is sometimes called the '''Gauss–Weierstrass kernel''', and is [[Green's function#Table of Green's functions|Green's function for the diffusion equation]] <math display="block">(\partial_t -D^2) (e^{tD^2} f(x))=0,</math> on <math>\R</math>.
<math>W_t</math> can be computed from <math>W</math>: given a function <math>f(x)</math>, define a new function <math display="block">f_t(x) := f(x\sqrt{t}),</math> then <math display="block">W_t[f](x) = W[f_t](x\sqrt{t}),</math> a consequence of the [[substitution rule]].

The Weierstrass transform can also be defined for certain classes of [[distribution (mathematics)|distribution]]s or "generalized functions".<ref>Yu A. Brychkov, A. P. Prudnikov. ''Integral Transforms of Generalized Functions'', Chapter 5. CRC Press, 1989</ref> For example, the Weierstrass transform of the [[Dirac delta]] is the Gaussian <math display="block">\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} e^{-x^2/4}.</math>
In this context, rigorous inversion formulas can be proved, e.g.,
<math display="block">f(x)=\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{i\sqrt{4\pi}} \int_{x_0-ir}^{x_0+ir} F(z)e^{\frac{(x-z)^2}{4}}\;dz,</math>
where <math>x_0</math> is any fixed [[real number]] for which <math>F(x_0)</math> exists, the integral extends over the vertical line in the complex plane with real part <math>x_0</math>, and the limit is to be taken in the sense of distributions.

Furthermore, the Weierstrass transform can be defined for real- (or complex-) valued functions (or distributions) defined on <math>\R^n</math>. We use the same convolution formula as above but interpret the integral as extending over all of <math>\R^n</math> and the expression <math>(x-y)^2</math> as the square of the [[Euclidean distance|Euclidean length]] of the vector <math>x-y</math>; the factor in front of the integral has to be adjusted so that the Gaussian will have a total integral of 1.

More generally, the Weierstrass transform can be defined on any [[Riemannian manifold]]: the heat equation can be formulated there (using the manifold's [[Laplace–Beltrami operator]]), and the Weierstrass transform <math>W[f]</math> is then given by following the solution of the heat equation for one time unit, starting with the initial "temperature distribution" <math>f</math>.

==Related transforms==
If one considers convolution with the kernel  <math>\frac{1}{(1+x^2)\pi}</math> instead of with a Gaussian, one obtains the [[Poisson kernel|Poisson transform]] which smoothes and averages a given function in a manner similar to the Weierstrass transform.
